subChunks.title: Output: System.out

storyBeats.text: Every wizard must be able to communicate their findings. In Java, your primary tool for speaking to the world is System.out.

storyBeats.speaker: Mentor
storyBeats.text: You already know println. But there's a whole family of output methods — and a powerful formatting tool called printf.

storyBeats.label: Output methods
storyBeats.code:
System.out.println("Hello!");   // prints + newline
System.out.print("Hello ");     // prints, no newline
System.out.print("World\n");    // manual newline
System.out.printf("Name: %s, Level: %d%n", "Eldrin", 99);

storyBeats.text: printf uses format specifiers: %s for strings, %d for integers, %f for floats, %.2f for 2 decimal places, %n for a platform-safe newline.

guidedPractice.problemHtml:
Print the following output using println and printf:

Name: Eldrin
Level: 99
Power: 9.50
guidedPractice.hint: Use println for the name and level lines, then printf with %.2f for the power line.

subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain the difference between print, println, and printf in your own words.

questions.prompt: Which format specifier is used for integers in printf?
questions.explanation: %d is the format specifier for integers (decimal). %s is for strings, %f is for floating-point numbers.

questions.prompt: System.out.println automatically adds a newline at the end.
questions.explanation: println stands for 'print line' — it always appends a newline character after the output.
%.1f rounds to 1 decimal place. 8.567 rounds up to 8.6.

questions.prompt: What is the difference between %n and \n in printf?
options: %n is platform-independent newline; \n is always Unix-style
questions.answer: %n is platform-independent newline; \n is always Unix-style
questions.explanation: %n outputs the system-appropriate newline (\r\n on Windows, \n on Unix), making your output portable across platforms.

subChunks.title: Input: Scanner Basics

storyBeats.text: Output is only half the conversation. To read from the user, you need Java's Scanner class.

storyBeats.speaker: Mentor
storyBeats.text: Scanner wraps an input source — usually System.in — and gives you methods to read different types of data.

storyBeats.label: Scanner setup

storyBeats.text: Key Scanner methods: nextLine() reads a full line, nextInt() reads an integer, nextDouble() reads a decimal. Always close the scanner when finished.

guidedPractice.problemHtml: Read a name and an age from input, then print: Hello, [name]! You are [age] years old.
guidedPractice.hint: Use nextLine() for the name and nextInt() for the age.

tests.label: Read name and age
tests.expected: Hello, Merlin! You are 42 years old.

subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Why do we need to import Scanner, but not System.out?

questions.prompt: Which Scanner method reads a complete line of text?
questions.explanation: nextLine() reads the entire line including spaces. next() only reads up to the first whitespace.

questions.prompt: You must import java.util.Scanner before using it.
questions.explanation: Scanner is in the java.util package and must be imported. Only java.lang classes (like String, System) are available without import.
Scanner must be imported from java.util. Without the import statement, the compiler won't find the Scanner class.

questions.prompt: Why should you call sc.close() when finished with a Scanner?
options: To release the underlying stream resource
To reset the scanner for reuse
questions.answer: To release the underlying stream resource
questions.explanation: Closing the Scanner releases the underlying input stream (System.in). Not closing it can cause resource leaks, especially when reading from files.

subChunks.title: Reading Different Types & Validation

storyBeats.text: Scanner can read many types, but mixing nextInt() and nextLine() has a notorious pitfall every Java apprentice must learn.

storyBeats.speaker: Mentor
storyBeats.text: When you call nextInt(), it reads the number but leaves the newline character in the buffer. The next nextLine() then picks up that leftover newline instead of waiting for real input.

storyBeats.label: The nextLine pitfall and fix

storyBeats.text: You can also validate input before reading with hasNextInt(), hasNextDouble() etc. These return true if the next token can be parsed as that type.

storyBeats.label: Safe integer reading

guidedPractice.problemHtml: Read two integers and print their sum.
guidedPractice.hint: Use nextInt() twice, then add and print.

subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Describe the nextLine-after-nextInt bug as if explaining to a friend who's never seen it before.

options: Returns true if the next token is a valid integer
Reads the next integer without consuming it
Checks if there is any more input
Validates that the entire input is an integer
questions.answer: Returns true if the next token is a valid integer
questions.explanation: hasNextInt() peeks at the next token and returns true if it can be parsed as an int, without actually consuming the input.

options: nextInt() leaves the newline in the buffer; nextLine() reads it
nextLine() can only be called once
age and name share the same buffer
questions.answer: nextInt() leaves the newline in the buffer; nextLine() reads it
questions.explanation: nextInt() reads the integer but stops at the newline. The following nextLine() immediately reads up to that leftover newline, returning empty string.

questions.prompt: What is the fix for the nextLine-after-nextInt problem?
options: Call sc.nextLine() once after nextInt() to consume the newline
questions.answer: Call sc.nextLine() once after nextInt() to consume the newline
questions.explanation: Adding an extra sc.nextLine() call after nextInt() (or any type-specific read) consumes the leftover newline, so the next nextLine() call waits for real input.

questions.prompt: When should you prefer sc.next() over sc.nextLine()?
options: When you want a single word (no spaces) and don't need the rest of the line
When you need the entire line including spaces
next() is always safer than nextLine()
questions.answer: When you want a single word (no spaces) and don't need the rest of the line
questions.explanation: next() reads up to the next whitespace — perfect for single tokens. nextLine() reads the entire line including spaces. Neither is 'safer'; they serve different purposes.
